lead: Edge beams, spandrel beams, ring beams and beams carrying sunshades feel bending, shear and torsion at the same section. IS 456 handles the three together with two equivalent actions. The equivalent moment M<sub>e1</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub> sizes the bars on the tension face, and M<sub>e2</sub> = M<sub>t</sub> − M<sub>u</sub> on the compression face when torsion is large. The equivalent shear V<sub>e</sub> checks the section and, with T<sub>u</sub> and V<sub>u</sub>, sizes the closed stirrups. Only a few syllabi list this as a topic of its own; it is where the torsion and the shear chapters come together into one complete beam design.
prereq: You need: Ve, Mt and the torsion stirrup formula from Design for torsion, and the singly reinforced beam design (limit state design of beams).

blocks.text: Torsion pulls on all four corner bars: the spiral struts of the space truss need a longitudinal tie. On the bottom face this tension adds to the bending tension, which is why M<sub>t</sub> is added to M<sub>u</sub>. On the top face bending causes compression, which cancels some of the torsion tension. If M<sub>t</sub> is larger than M<sub>u</sub>, the top face ends up in net tension, which is the case IS 456 covers with M<sub>e2</sub>.

Shear and torsion shear add on one side face and subtract on the other. The equivalent shear V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b is the side that adds, so checking τ<sub>ve</sub> against τ<sub>c,max</sub> protects the worst face against web crushing.
M<sub>e1</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + T<sub>u</sub> (1 + D/b)/1.7          M<sub>e2</sub> = M<sub>t</sub> − M<sub>u</sub> (when M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub>)
blocks.where: M<sub>e1</sub> is the equivalent moment for the flexural tension face (kN·m); M<sub>e2</sub> acts in the opposite sense and is designed on the flexural compression face (kN·m); D/b is the overall depth over the breadth, no unit.

items: Find the factored M<sub>u</sub>, V<sub>u</sub> and T<sub>u</sub> at the section, and decide that the torsion is equilibrium torsion.
Find V<sub>e</sub> and τ<sub>ve</sub> = V<sub>e</sub>/(b d). If τ<sub>ve</sub> > τ<sub>c,max</sub>, enlarge the section.
Find M<sub>t</sub> and M<sub>e1</sub>. Check M<sub>e1</sub> ≤ M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² (Fe415); if larger, design a doubly reinforced section.

Find A<sub>st</sub> for M<sub>e1</sub> from M = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> d (1 − A<sub>st</sub> f<sub>y</sub>/(b d f<sub>ck</sub>)), or from the SP 16 flexure table using M<sub>e1</sub>/(b d²).
If M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub>, find the steel for M<sub>e2</sub> on the other face.

Read τ<sub>c</sub> for the steel provided; if τ<sub>ve</sub> > τ<sub>c</sub>, design closed stirrups from the torsion formula, check the (τ<sub>ve</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub>) b s<sub>v</sub>/(0.87 f<sub>y</sub>) lower limit and the spacing limits x<sub>1</sub>, (x<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>1</sub>)/4 and 300 mm.

Detail: a bar in every corner, side-face bars when D exceeds 450 mm (0.1 % of the web area, shared between the two faces, at 300 mm or less), 135° hooks, and full anchorage of the longitudinal bars at the supports.

blocks.text: The factors 1.6 and 1.7 are calibrated against tests on rectangular beams, not derived from statics; use them as given, with consistent units.

examples.question: Complete the design of the edge beam of the previous chapter at the section where M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kN·m, V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m. b = 300 mm, D = 600 mm, d = 550 mm, M25, Fe415, nominal cover 30 mm, 10 mm stirrups.
steps: M<sub>t</sub> = 30 × (1 + 600/300)/1.7 = 30 × 3/1.7 = 52.94 kN·m. Since M<sub>t</sub> < M<sub>u</sub>, no steel is needed for M<sub>e2</sub>.
M<sub>e1</sub> = 150 + 52.94 = 202.94 kN·m. M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 25 × 300 × 550² = 313.1 kN·m, so the section is singly reinforced.

Tension steel: 202.94 × 10⁶ = 0.87 × 415 × A<sub>st</sub> × 550 × (1 − 415 A<sub>st</sub>/(300 × 550 × 25)) gives A<sub>st</sub> = 1157 mm². (M<sub>e1</sub>/(b d²) = 2.24 N/mm² and the SP 16 flexure table for M25 and Fe415 gives p<sub>t</sub> ≈ 0.70 %, the same answer.)
Top: two 12 mm corner bars (226 mm²) to hold the stirrups and act as torsion stringers.
Side faces: D = 600 mm > 450 mm, so provide 0.1 % × 300 × 600 = 180 mm², that is one 12 mm bar on each face (113 mm² each) at mid-depth; the gaps are about 250 mm, below 300 mm.
Shear and torsion (from the previous chapter): V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN, τ<sub>ve</sub> = 1.70 N/mm², τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 N/mm²; closed 10 mm stirrups at 140 mm.
Final section: 4 bars of 20 mm at the bottom, 2 of 12 mm at the top, 1 of 12 mm on each side face, 10 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm with 135° hooks.
examples.answer: M<sub>e1</sub> = 202.94 kN·m needs 1157 mm²: four 20 mm bars (1257 mm², M<sub>R</sub> = 217.8 kN·m). Two 12 mm top bars, one 12 mm bar on each side face, and 10 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm.

examples.question: Near the support of the same beam, M<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m while V<sub>u</sub> and T<sub>u</sub> are still 120 kN and 30 kN·m. Is steel needed on the top face, and are the bars of worked example 1 enough there?
steps: M<sub>t</sub> = 52.94 kN·m as before. Now M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m.
Bottom face: M<sub>e1</sub> = 30 + 52.94 = 82.94 kN·m, needing A<sub>st</sub> = 437 mm². The four 20 mm bars (1257 mm²) continue to the support, so this is met.

Top face: M<sub>e2</sub> = 52.94 − 30 = 22.94 kN·m acting in the opposite sense, so the top face is in tension. Taking the top bars at an effective depth of 600 − 46 = 554 mm, the steel needed is 116 mm².

The two 12 mm top bars give 226 mm² > 116 mm², so they are enough, but they are now tension bars: they must run continuously and be anchored into the support with full development length, not stopped as hanger bars.
examples.answer: Yes: M<sub>t</sub> = 52.94 > M<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m, so M<sub>e2</sub> = 22.94 kN·m needs 116 mm² on the top face. The two 12 mm top bars (226 mm²) are enough if they are continuous and fully anchored; the bottom face needs 437 mm² for M<sub>e1</sub> = 82.94 kN·m.

traps: Designing the bottom steel for M<sub>u</sub> alone. The tension face is designed for M<sub>e1</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub>.
Forgetting M<sub>e2</sub> near supports or wherever M<sub>u</sub> is small. When M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub>, the top face is in tension and its bars must be designed and anchored as tension bars.

Designing the stirrups for V<sub>e</sub> with the ordinary shear formula. With torsion, A<sub>sv</sub> comes from T<sub>u</sub> s<sub>v</sub>/(b<sub>1</sub> d<sub>1</sub> 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>) + V<sub>u</sub> s<sub>v</sub>/(2.5 d<sub>1</sub> 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>), with V<sub>e</sub> used only for τ<sub>ve</sub> and the lower limit.
Leaving out the side-face bars of a beam deeper than 450 mm under torsion.
Writing M<sub>t</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> (1 + b/D)/1.7. The ratio is D/b, overall depth over breadth: 2.0 here, not 0.5.

quiz.q: When is M<sub>e2</sub> needed and on which face is it designed?
quiz.a: When M<sub>t</sub> exceeds M<sub>u</sub>. M<sub>e2</sub> = M<sub>t</sub> − M<sub>u</sub> acts opposite to M<sub>u</sub> and is designed on the flexural compression face.

quiz.q: Why is M<sub>t</sub> added to M<sub>u</sub> on the tension face?
quiz.a: After cracking, the spiral struts of the space truss need a longitudinal tie at every corner. On the tension face this torsion tension adds to the bending tension, so the bars there must carry both.

quiz.q: b = 250 mm, D = 500 mm, M<sub>u</sub> = 80 kN·m, T<sub>u</sub> = 20 kN·m. Find M<sub>t</sub>, M<sub>e1</sub> and whether M<sub>e2</sub> is needed.
quiz.a: M<sub>t</sub> = 20 × (1 + 2)/1.7 = 35.29 kN·m. M<sub>e1</sub> = 80 + 35.29 = 115.29 kN·m. M<sub>t</sub> < M<sub>u</sub>, so no M<sub>e2</sub>.

quiz.q: For the beam of the previous question near a support where M<sub>u</sub> = 10 kN·m, find M<sub>e2</sub>.
quiz.a: M<sub>t</sub> = 35.29 > 10 kN·m, so M<sub>e2</sub> = 35.29 − 10 = 25.29 kN·m on the top face.

quiz.q: In worked example 1, the strength needs stirrups at 144 mm while (τ<sub>ve</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub>) gives 168 mm. Which governs and why are there two checks?
quiz.a: 144 mm governs because it is smaller. The first check is the torsion and shear demand on the closed stirrups; the second makes sure the stirrups are never less than what the ordinary shear route would give for the equivalent shear, a floor for cases with small torque.

quiz.q: Why can a beam satisfy the flexure design for M<sub>u</sub> and still fail in a sunshade loading case?
quiz.a: The sunshade adds torque. Without torsion design the beam lacks closed stirrups and the extra longitudinal steel for M<sub>t</sub>, so it can crack in a spiral and fail by skew bending even though M<sub>u</sub> alone is safe.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design software checks each section of a frame for combined actions automatically, but engineers still hand-check edge beams that support cantilevers, because a missed torque there gives no warning. Research on combined loading builds interaction surfaces of bending, shear and torsion from tests and space truss theory. Precast spandrel beams in car parks are a well-known case of large equilibrium torsion. Search for 'interaction of bending shear and torsion', 'spandrel beam torsion' and 'skew bending theory'.
